prompt: Match each provider to its model family, as at the time of writing.
hint: The table in the first section.

prompt: Why does this lesson give no version numbers, prices or scores?
hint: Which facts about models change fastest?

choices.text: Providers forbid courses from publishing them
choices.why: Nothing forbids it. They would simply be wrong soon.

choices.text: They are the same for every provider, so there is nothing to compare
choices.why: They differ a great deal, and they change.

choices.text: Version numbers and prices are secret until a model is retired
choices.why: They are published, and that is why they are easy to check at the source.

choices.text: They go stale first
choices.why: Right. Names, prices and scores change within months; the shape of each provider's offer lasts longer.

prompt: A colleague says: "We use GPT, so we know which model we are on." What does this lesson say is missing?
hint: How many models is one family?

choices.text: Nothing: one family is one model
choices.why: Each family is many models, released and retired over time.

choices.text: The region, which decides the family
choices.why: Region decides availability, not which model you call.

choices.text: The family has several models, of different sizes
choices.why: Right. A family name says which company; the exact model decides cost, speed and quality.

choices.text: The tokenizer, which is the same for every model
choices.why: Tokenizers differ between models; and the missing fact is which model it is.

prompt: Which of these providers offers a family of open-weight models alongside a closed one?
hint: The table names one family as separate and downloadable.

choices.text: Anthropic, with Claude
choices.why: Claude is reached through apps, the API and cloud platforms. Its weights are not published.

choices.text: Google, with Gemma beside Gemini
choices.why: Right. Gemini is used through Google's services; Gemma's weights are downloadable.

choices.text: xAI, with Grok, whose current models are downloadable
choices.why: xAI published the weights of an earlier Grok model, not its current ones.

choices.text: Meta, whose Llama weights are closed
choices.why: Llama weights are downloadable, under Meta's own licence.

prompt: What does this lesson say about reasoning models?
hint: What do they do before the final answer, and what does it cost?

choices.text: They are a sixth provider
choices.why: They are a kind of model several providers offer.

choices.text: More tokens and time per answer, in exchange for many-step problems
choices.why: Right. They write a long chain of intermediate steps first, which helps with mathematics and code and is billed.

choices.text: They are cheaper because they think instead of writing
choices.why: The thinking is written out as tokens, which is why they cost more per answer.

choices.text: They do not predict tokens
choices.why: They are still next-token predictors, trained to write steps first.

prompt: Which of these are true of the field, according to this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last part of the first section.

choices.text: Providers outside the five publish widely used open-weight models
choices.why: Yes: Mistral AI, DeepSeek and Alibaba's Qwen team among them.

choices.text: One model can be sold through more than one platform
choices.why: Yes, with different prices, limits, regions and data terms on each.

choices.text: The five in the title are the only serious providers
choices.why: The lesson says choosing only among them is choosing from part of the menu.

choices.text: A family name tells you the model's exact price
choices.why: Prices are per exact model, and they change.

hint: After lesson 8, what is the whole model?

choices.text: Its training data is published in full
choices.why: That would be closer to open source. Most open-weight models do not publish it.

choices.text: It is free to call through an API
choices.why: Price has nothing to do with it. Some closed models are free to try.

choices.text: Anyone can change how the provider's service behaves
choices.why: Nobody changes a provider's service. Open weights are a file you hold.

choices.text: You can download its weights
choices.why: Right. The weights are the model, so downloading them means you can run it yourself.

prompt: Why does this course say "open weights" rather than "open source" for most such models?
hint: What else would you need to rebuild the model?

choices.text: Open source means free of charge
choices.why: Open source is about being able to study, change and share, not price.

choices.text: The weights are encrypted
choices.why: Downloaded weights are a readable file of numbers.

choices.text: Only the weights are published
choices.why: Right. The data and training code that made them are not, and without them nobody can rebuild the model or check what it learnt from.

choices.text: Open source is only for software written in Python
choices.why: It applies to software in any language.

prompt: You run an open-weight model on your own server. Which question from the data section is answered by that alone?

choices.text: Whether the licence allows your use
choices.why: The licence still has to be read, for the exact model.

choices.text: Whether the model is good enough for your task
choices.why: Only your own test set answers that.

choices.text: Whether your prompts leave your machine
choices.why: Right. They do not: nothing is sent to a provider.

choices.text: How much memory it needs
choices.why: That is arithmetic you still have to do, lesson 8.

prompt: Two releases from the same provider are both described as open. What does this lesson tell you to do before using one in a product?

choices.text: Read a summary of the family's licence
choices.why: Two releases can carry different terms. A family summary is not enough.

choices.text: Read the licence of that exact release
choices.why: Right. Licences differ even within one provider, and can restrict size of company, uses or naming.

choices.text: Nothing, since open means no conditions
choices.why: Many open-weight licences carry conditions.

choices.text: Ask the model what its licence says
choices.why: Its reply is generated text, not the licence.

prompt: Your company forbids customer data leaving its own servers. Which arrangement fits, and what does it cost you?
hint: The table of two ways to use a model.

choices.text: Open weights on your own hardware
choices.why: Right. The data stays in, and you take on the hardware, the arithmetic of lesson 8 and the upkeep.

choices.text: A closed model through its API, with a promise in the prompt
choices.why: A promise in a prompt does not stop the prompt itself reaching the provider.

choices.text: An open-weight model through a cloud company's API
choices.why: That is someone else's hardware. The data leaves your servers.

choices.text: A consumer chat app, with history switched off
choices.why: The data still goes to the provider to be answered.

prompt: Which of these should you check in a provider's own documents before sending it customer data? Choose all that apply.
hint: The four questions of the data section.

choices.text: Whether data is stored, and for how long
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Whether it is used to train future models
choices.why: Yes, and whether that can be switched off.

choices.text: In which countries it is processed
choices.why: Yes, against the rules you work under.

choices.text: Which model family has the highest benchmark score
choices.why: A score is not a data question, and it ages fast.

prompt: How many tokens does `cl100k_base` make of "O café abre às oito aos domingos."?
hint: Read the last line of the first capture.

prompt: And how many does `o200k_base` make of the same sentence?
Provider A charges less per million tokens than provider B. Why can you not conclude that A is cheaper for your task?
hint: What did `tok show` do to one sentence?

choices.text: Prices per million tokens are not published
choices.why: They are published. They are just not comparable across tokenizers.

choices.text: The same text is a different number of tokens at each
choices.why: Right. Compare the cost of a whole typical request instead.

choices.text: A is cheaper; the lesson only warns about latency
choices.why: The lesson's point is that per-token prices do not compare, because tokens differ.

choices.text: Every provider uses the same tokenizer, so the difference is a mistake
choices.why: Even one provider has two encodings that disagree, as the captures show.

prompt: What does this lesson say is the most reliable way to judge quality for your use?

choices.text: Your own cases, run on each candidate
choices.why: Right. Your inputs, your edge cases, and nobody trained on them.

choices.text: The top of a public leaderboard
choices.why: Someone else's tasks, possibly in the training data (lesson 10).

choices.text: The newest model from the largest provider
choices.why: Newest and largest are not measurements of your task.

choices.text: The model card's description of what it is good at
choices.why: The card is the best source for facts about the model; quality on your task is yours to measure.

prompt: Order the sources of information about a model from most to least trusted.
hint: The list in the last section.
items: The model card for the exact model
The provider's dated documentation and pricing pages

prompt: A course you are reading has a table ranking five models by price and quality, dated two years ago. How should you use it?
hint: What goes stale, and what does not?

choices.text: As the answer, since rankings change slowly
choices.why: Rankings, prices and names change within months.

choices.text: Not at all, since everything in it is false
choices.why: Some of it may still hold. It is a pointer, not a source.

choices.text: As proof of which provider to sign with
choices.why: A two-year-old table proves nothing about today's models.

choices.text: As a list of names to check in dated provider documents
choices.why: Right. The names may help you look; the prices and rankings are almost certainly out of date.
